questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION A: PURE MATHEMATICS**

If $\dfrac{M}{x-1}+\dfrac{N}{x+2}\equiv\dfrac{2x-1}{(x-1)(x+2)}$, then
questions.corrige_markdown:
Multiply both sides by $(x-1)(x+2)$: $M(x+2)+N(x-1)\equiv 2x-1$.

Put $x=1$: $3M=1$, so $M=\dfrac13$. Put $x=-2$: $-3N=-5$, so $N=\dfrac53$.

Check by comparing coefficients: $x$: $M+N=\dfrac13+\dfrac53=2$ (correct); constant: $2M-N=\dfrac23-\dfrac53=-1$ (correct).

Option A has the wrong sign for $N$ (it would give $M+N=-\frac43\neq2$); C and D do not satisfy $M+N=2$ and $2M-N=-1$ together.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given the function $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, where $f(x)=\dfrac{x+1}{x+2},\ x\neq-2$, the range of $f$ does not include the element
questions.corrige_markdown:
Write $f(x)=\dfrac{x+1}{x+2}=1-\dfrac{1}{x+2}$ (for $x\neq-2$). The term $\dfrac1{x+2}$ is never $0$, so $f(x)$ is never equal to $1$; it takes every other real value.

Algebraic check: put $y=\dfrac{x+1}{x+2}$. Then $y(x+2)=x+1$, so $x(y-1)=1-2y$ and $x=\dfrac{1-2y}{y-1}$, which exists exactly when $y\neq1$. The value $y=1$ would need $x+1=x+2$, which is impossible.

The other options are attained: $f(-3)=2$, $f\left(-\tfrac53\right)=-2$, $f\left(-\tfrac32\right)=-1$. The number $-2$ is the value excluded from the **domain** (denominator zero), not from the range, which is the usual trap.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The values of $x$ that satisfy the equation $2^{2x}-5\left(2^{x+1}\right)+2^{4}=0$ are
questions.corrige_markdown:
Use $2^{2x}=(2^x)^2$ and $2^{x+1}=2\cdot2^x$. Put $u=2^x>0$:
$u^2-10u+16=0\iff(u-2)(u-8)=0$, so $u=2$ or $u=8$.

Then $2^x=2$ gives $x=1$ and $2^x=8$ gives $x=3$. Both values are valid because $2^x>0$ always.

Check: $x=1$: $4-5\cdot4+16=0$. $x=3$: $64-5\cdot16+16=0$. Options with $-1$ or $-3$ would need $2^x=\frac12$ or $\frac18$, which do not satisfy the quadratic.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The solution of the differential equation $y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3x$, given that $y=1$ when $x=1$, is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Separate the variables: $y\,dy=3x\,dx$. Integrate: $\dfrac{y^2}{2}=\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+c$, i.e. $y^2=3x^2+k$ with $k=2c$.

Use $y=1$ when $x=1$: $1=3+k$, so $k=-2$. Hence $y^2=3x^2-2$.

Check: differentiating $y^2=3x^2-2$ gives $2y\,y'=6x$, i.e. $y\,y'=3x$. The other options do not satisfy the condition: with $x=1$, B gives $y^2=4$, C gives $y^2=2$, D gives $y^2=5$, none equal to $1$.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In the set $A=\{0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7\}$, a relation $\mathrm R$ is defined by $x\,\mathrm R\,y\Leftrightarrow x$ and $y$ have the same remainder when divided by $3$. The equivalence class of $3$, i.e. $[3]$, is
questions.corrige_markdown:
$[3]$ is the set of all $y\in A$ with $3\,\mathrm R\,y$, i.e. with the same remainder as $3$ on division by $3$. Since $3=3\cdot1+0$, the remainder is $0$.

The elements of $A$ with remainder $0$ are $0,3,6$ (the next one, $9$, is not in $A$). So $[3]=\{0,3,6\}$.

Option A forgets $0$ (which is in $A$); B is the class of $1$ (remainder 1); C is the class of $2$ (remainder 2).

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The line segment $PQ$, where $P$ is the point $(2,4)$ and $Q$ is the point $(8,10)$, is the diameter of a circle. The equation of the circle is
questions.corrige_markdown:
A point $X(x,y)$ lies on the circle with diameter $PQ$ exactly when the angle $PXQ$ is a right angle (Thales), i.e. $\overrightarrow{XP}\cdot\overrightarrow{XQ}=0$:
$(2-x)(8-x)+(4-y)(10-y)=0$, which is $(x-2)(x-8)+(y-4)(y-10)=0$.

Check: expanding gives $x^2-10x+16+y^2-14y+40=0$, i.e. $(x-5)^2+(y-7)^2=18$. The centre is the midpoint $(5,7)$ of $PQ$ and the radius is $\tfrac12PQ=\tfrac12\sqrt{6^2+6^2}=3\sqrt2$, so $r^2=18$.

Options B and D have a minus sign between the two products, which is a hyperbola, not a circle; C mixes up the coordinates of $P$ and $Q$.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: When $f(x)=2x^3+x^2-13x+6$ is divided by $2x+1$, the remainder is
questions.corrige_markdown:
By the remainder theorem, the remainder on division by $2x+1$ is $f\left(-\tfrac12\right)$ (the root of $2x+1=0$).

$f\left(-\tfrac12\right)=2\left(-\tfrac18\right)+\tfrac14+\tfrac{13}{2}+6=-\tfrac14+\tfrac14+6.5+6=12.5$.

Check by division: $2x^3+x^2-13x+6=(2x+1)\left(x^2-6.5\right)+12.5$. Option A would mean that $2x+1$ is a factor, which is false since $f\left(-\frac12\right)\neq0$.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The range of values of $x$ for which $|x-4|\geq2$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
$|x-4|\geq2$ means that $x$ is at distance at least $2$ from $4$: $x-4\geq2$ or $x-4\leq-2$, i.e. $x\geq6$ or $x\leq2$.

Option C is the solution of the opposite inequality $|x-4|\leq2$; A and B each keep only one half of the condition (and A and B both contain values such as $x=4$ that fail the inequality).

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Consider the two statements below.

$p$: John is sick.

$q$: He goes to the hospital.

The contrapositive of $p\Rightarrow q$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The contrapositive of $p\Rightarrow q$ is $\sim q\Rightarrow\sim p$: it is logically equivalent to the original implication ("if he does not go to the hospital, then John is not sick").

Option A is the converse and C is the inverse (neither is equivalent to $p\Rightarrow q$); B is neither.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $f(x)=\begin{vmatrix}0&2&x^2\\0&1&x^2\\1&3x&2x^2\end{vmatrix}$, $f'(x)=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Expand the determinant along the first column: its only non-zero entry is the $1$ in row 3, column 1, with sign $(-1)^{3+1}=+1$:
$f(x)=1\cdot\begin{vmatrix}2&x^2\\1&x^2\end{vmatrix}=2x^2-x^2=x^2$.

Hence $f'(x)=2x$.

Option C ($2x^2$) is not a derivative of $x^2$; B and D come from wrong expansions of the determinant.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $f$ is a periodic function of period $4$ and that $f(x)=\begin{cases}9-x^2, & 0<x\leq2\\ 3x-1, & 2<x\leq4\end{cases}$, $f(19)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Period $4$ means $f(x+4)=f(x)$, so $f(19)=f(19-4\cdot4)=f(3)$.

Since $2<3\leq4$, the second branch applies: $f(3)=3\cdot3-1=8$.

The tempting wrong answers use the formulas directly at $19$ (which lies outside the defining interval $(0,4]$): $3\cdot19-1=56$ (A) and $9-19^2=-352$ (B). Option C is the first branch evaluated at $3$ ($9-9=0$), but $3$ is not in $(0,2]$.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The volume generated when the area of the finite region enclosed by the $x$-axis and the curve $y=1-x^2$ is rotated completely about the $x$-axis is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The curve $y=1-x^2$ meets the $x$-axis at $x=\pm1$, so the finite region lies between $x=-1$ and $x=1$ (above the axis).

Rotating about the $x$-axis, a thin slice at abscissa $x$ is a disc of radius $y=1-x^2$ and volume $\pi y^2\,dx$. Therefore $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}(1-x^2)^2\,dx$ (value $\frac{16\pi}{15}$).

Option A covers only half of the region (from $0$ to $1$); B doubles the volume with a wrong factor $2\pi$; D uses $y$ instead of $y^2$ (with a factor $2\pi$ that belongs to a rotation about the $y$-axis by shells), so it does not give the volume.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
If a root of an equation $f(x)=0$ lies between $0$ and $1$, then

*Options as printed:* A) $f(0)f(1)\leq0$   B) $f(0)f(1)>0$   C) $f(0)f(1)\geq0$   D) $f(0)f(1)<0$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Take $f$ continuous. A root strictly between $0$ and $1$ is detected by a change of sign of $f$ on $[0,1]$: $f(0)$ and $f(1)$ have opposite signs, i.e. $f(0)f(1)<0$. This is the criterion of the intermediate value theorem used to locate a root.

Options B and C describe the same sign at both ends (no sign change). Option A also holds when $f(0)f(1)<0$, but it is weaker: it allows $f(0)=0$ or $f(1)=0$, a root at an end-point and not between.

Note on the question as printed: a root between $0$ and $1$ does not by itself force a sign change (for example $f(x)=(x-0.5)^2$ has a double root at $0.5$ and $f(0)f(1)>0$); the question is meant as the sign-change test, whose expected form is D.

**Intended answer: D ($f(0)f(1)<0$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The vectors $\mathbf p$ and $\mathbf q$ are such that $|\mathbf p|=3$, $|\mathbf q|=5$ and $\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf q=-14$. The value of $|\mathbf p-\mathbf q|=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Expand the square of the length: $|\mathbf p-\mathbf q|^2=(\mathbf p-\mathbf q)\cdot(\mathbf p-\mathbf q)=|\mathbf p|^2-2\,\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf q+|\mathbf q|^2=9-2(-14)+25=62$.

So $|\mathbf p-\mathbf q|=\sqrt{62}$.

Option D ($62$) is $|\mathbf p-\mathbf q|^2$, the value before taking the square root. (The data are consistent: $\cos\theta=\frac{-14}{15}$ lies between $-1$ and $1$.)

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The sum of the first $n$ terms of a sequence is given by $S_n=2n^2+n$. The $n^{\text{th}}$ term of the sequence is
questions.corrige_markdown:
For $n\geq2$: $u_n=S_n-S_{n-1}=(2n^2+n)-\left[2(n-1)^2+(n-1)\right]=2n^2+n-2n^2+4n-2-n+1=4n-1$.

For $n=1$: $u_1=S_1=3$, and $4\cdot1-1=3$, so the formula also holds for $n=1$. Hence $u_n=4n-1$ for all $n\geq1$ (an arithmetic sequence with common difference $4$).

Check: $u_1+u_2=3+7=10=S_2=2\cdot4+2$. Option C gives $u_1=5\neq S_1$.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The expansion of $(3+5x)^{-2}$ is valid when
questions.corrige_markdown:
Factor out the constant term: $(3+5x)^{-2}=3^{-2}\left(1+\dfrac{5x}{3}\right)^{-2}$.

The binomial series for $(1+z)^{-2}$ converges if and only if $|z|<1$ (at $z=\pm1$ the terms $(n+1)(\mp1)^n$ do not tend to $0$, so the series diverges at both ends). With $z=\dfrac{5x}{3}$: $\left|\dfrac{5x}{3}\right|<1\iff-\dfrac35<x<\dfrac35$, with strict inequalities.

Options A, C and D include one or both end-points, where the series diverges.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The Cartesian equation of the curve with parametric equation $x=2t,\ y=\dfrac2t$, where $t$ is a parameter is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Eliminate $t$: from $x=2t$, $t=\dfrac x2$ ($x\neq0$). Then $y=\dfrac{2}{t}=\dfrac{2}{x/2}=\dfrac4x$.

Check: $xy=2t\cdot\dfrac2t=4$ for every $t\neq0$, so the curve is the rectangular hyperbola $xy=4$. Option B would be $xy=1$ and option C would be $4y=x$.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to1}\left(\dfrac{x^2-1}{x-1}\right)=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Both numerator and denominator tend to $0$ (form $\frac00$), so factorise: $\dfrac{x^2-1}{x-1}=\dfrac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1}=x+1$ for $x\neq1$.

Hence the limit is $\lim_{x\to1}(x+1)=2$. (Equivalently, it is the derivative of $x^2$ at $x=1$.)

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\dfrac12+\dfrac14+\dfrac18+\dfrac1{16}+\cdots=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
This is a geometric series with first term $a=\dfrac12$ and common ratio $r=\dfrac12$, with $|r|<1$, so it converges to $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}=\dfrac{1/2}{1/2}=1$.

Check with partial sums: $S_n=1-\dfrac1{2^n}\to1$. Option C ($2$) is the sum of $1+\frac12+\frac14+\cdots$, which starts at $1$ instead of $\frac12$.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The asymptotes of the curve $y=\dfrac{1}{x^2-5x+6}$ are
questions.corrige_markdown:
Factorise the denominator: $x^2-5x+6=(x-2)(x-3)$. It vanishes at $x=2$ and $x=3$, where the numerator is $1\neq0$, so $x=2$ and $x=3$ are vertical asymptotes.

As $x\to\pm\infty$, $y=\dfrac1{x^2-5x+6}\to0$ (the degree of the numerator is less than that of the denominator), so $y=0$ is the horizontal asymptote.

Options A and C use roots of the wrong sign (they would come from $x^2+5x+6$); options C and D give $y=1$ as horizontal asymptote, but $y\to0$, not $1$.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The values of $y$ corresponding to the values of $x$ are given in the table below.

| $x$ | 6 | 9 | 12 | 15 | 18 | 21 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $y$ | 0.3 | 0.8 | $a$ | 2.1 | 3.0 | 4.3 |

Using the trapezium rule, $\displaystyle\int_6^{21}y\,dx\approx28.8$. The value of $a$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
There are $6$ ordinates, so $5$ strips of width $h=3$. The trapezium rule gives
$\displaystyle\int_6^{21}y\,dx\approx\dfrac h2\Big[y_0+y_5+2(y_1+y_2+y_3+y_4)\Big]=\dfrac32\Big[0.3+4.3+2(0.8+a+2.1+3.0)\Big]$.

Simplify: $\dfrac32\left[4.6+11.8+2a\right]=\dfrac32(16.4+2a)=24.6+3a$.

Set equal to $28.8$: $3a=4.2$, so $a=1.4$.

Check: $\frac32\left[4.6+2(0.8+1.4+2.1+3.0)\right]=\frac32(4.6+14.6)=28.8$. Option C ($1.8$) would give $30.0$.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The gradient of the implicit function $2x+xy=5$ at the point $(1,1)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$, using the product rule on $xy$: $2+y+x\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{2+y}{x}$.

At $(1,1)$: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{2+1}{1}=-3$.

Note: the point $(1,1)$ does not lie exactly on the curve ($2\cdot1+1\cdot1=3\neq5$); the question is answered by evaluating the derivative formula at the given coordinates, which is the only reading that gives one of the options.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\sin35^\circ+\sin25^\circ=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Use the sum-to-product formula $\sin A+\sin B=2\sin\dfrac{A+B}{2}\cos\dfrac{A-B}{2}$:
$\sin35^\circ+\sin25^\circ=2\sin30^\circ\cos5^\circ=2\cdot\dfrac12\cos5^\circ=\cos5^\circ$.

Numerical check: $\sin35^\circ+\sin25^\circ=0.57358+0.42262=0.99619=\cos5^\circ$. Option A forgets that $\sin30^\circ=\frac12$.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that the plane $\mu x-2y+5z=6$ and the line $\mathbf r=2\mathbf i-3\mathbf j+\mathbf k+s(\mathbf i-2\mathbf j+3\mathbf k)$ are parallel, find the value of the constant $\mu$.
questions.corrige_markdown:
A normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf n=\mu\mathbf i-2\mathbf j+5\mathbf k$ and the direction of the line is $\mathbf d=\mathbf i-2\mathbf j+3\mathbf k$. The line is parallel to the plane exactly when $\mathbf d\perp\mathbf n$, i.e. $\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf d=0$:
$\mu\cdot1+(-2)(-2)+5\cdot3=\mu+4+15=0$, so $\mu=-19$.

Check that the line is parallel and not contained in the plane: the point $(2,-3,1)$ gives $-19\cdot2+6+5=-27\neq6$, so it is not in the plane.

Option B is the result of a sign error ($\mu=+19$).

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{x}{2+3x^2}\,dx=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The derivative of the denominator is $\dfrac{d}{dx}(2+3x^2)=6x$, so the numerator $x$ is $\dfrac16$ of it. Using $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}dx=\ln|f(x)|+c$:
$\displaystyle\int\dfrac{x}{2+3x^2}dx=\dfrac16\int\dfrac{6x}{2+3x^2}dx=\dfrac16\ln(2+3x^2)+K$ (the modulus is not needed since $2+3x^2>0$).

Check: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\dfrac16\ln(2+3x^2)\right]=\dfrac16\cdot\dfrac{6x}{2+3x^2}=\dfrac{x}{2+3x^2}$. Option A forgets the factor $\frac16$; B multiplies by $6$ instead of dividing.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The general solution of the equation $\cos\left(2x+\dfrac\pi3\right)=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
$\cos\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt3}2$ has the general solution $\theta=2n\pi\pm\dfrac\pi6$ ($n\in\mathbb Z$), since $\cos\dfrac\pi6=\dfrac{\sqrt3}2$ and cosine is even and $2\pi$-periodic.

Here $\theta=2x+\dfrac\pi3$, so $2x+\dfrac\pi3=2n\pi\pm\dfrac\pi6$, i.e. $2x=2n\pi\pm\dfrac\pi6-\dfrac\pi3$ (both signs).

Check: $x=-\dfrac\pi{12}$ (the "+" branch, $n=0$): $2x+\frac\pi3=-\frac\pi6+\frac\pi3=\frac\pi6$ and $\cos\frac\pi6=\frac{\sqrt3}2$. Also $x=-\dfrac\pi4$ (the "-" branch): $2x+\frac\pi3=-\frac\pi6$, $\cos(-\frac\pi6)=\frac{\sqrt3}2$. Option B keeps only the "+" branch, so it misses half of the solutions; C and D are not solutions in general.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The Cartesian equation of the line $\mathbf r=\mathbf i-\mathbf j+6\mathbf k+\mu(-5\mathbf i+\mathbf j-4\mathbf k)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The line passes through the point with position vector $\mathbf i-\mathbf j+6\mathbf k$, i.e. $(1,-1,6)$, with direction vector $-5\mathbf i+\mathbf j-4\mathbf k$, i.e. $(-5,1,-4)$.

Eliminating $\mu$ from $x=1-5\mu$, $y=-1+\mu$, $z=6-4\mu$ gives $\dfrac{x-1}{-5}=\dfrac{y+1}{1}=\dfrac{z-6}{-4}\;(=\mu)$.

Check with $\mu=1$: the point $(-4,0,2)$ gives $\frac{-5}{-5}=\frac{1}{1}=\frac{-4}{-4}=1$. Options A and B swap the roles of point and direction; D has the opposite point $(-1,1,-6)$.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If the sequence $u_n$ where $n\in\mathbb N$ is strictly monotonic increasing then
questions.corrige_markdown:
A sequence is strictly increasing when each term is strictly larger than the previous one: $u_{n+1}>u_n$ for all $n$.

A and B describe a (strictly) decreasing / non-increasing sequence; D ($u_{n+1}\geq u_n$) is "increasing" in the weak sense (constant stretches allowed), not strictly.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A bijective function is that which is
questions.corrige_markdown:
A function $f:E\to F$ is bijective when it is both injective (different elements have different images) and surjective (every element of $F$ has a pre-image); then every element of $F$ has exactly one pre-image and $f$ has an inverse.

A describes an equivalence relation (a property of relations, not of functions); C adds an irrelevant property; D describes sequences.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The complex number $z=1+i$ can be expressed in exponential form as
questions.corrige_markdown:
Modulus: $|z|=\sqrt{1^2+1^2}=\sqrt2$. Argument: $z$ is in the first quadrant with $\tan\theta=\dfrac11=1$, so $\theta=\dfrac\pi4$.

Hence $z=\sqrt2\,e^{i\pi/4}$. Check: $\sqrt2\left(\cos\frac\pi4+i\sin\frac\pi4\right)=\sqrt2\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}2(1+i)=1+i$.

Option A has modulus $1$, B has argument $-\frac\pi4$ (that is $1-i$ up to modulus), D has modulus $2$.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\dfrac{\cos5\theta+i\sin5\theta}{(\cos2\theta+i\sin2\theta)^{-3}}=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
By de Moivre's theorem, $(\cos2\theta+i\sin2\theta)^{-3}=\cos(-6\theta)+i\sin(-6\theta)=\cos6\theta-i\sin6\theta=e^{-6i\theta}$, and $\cos5\theta+i\sin5\theta=e^{5i\theta}$.

Dividing by $e^{-6i\theta}$ means multiplying by $e^{6i\theta}$: $\dfrac{e^{5i\theta}}{e^{-6i\theta}}=e^{11i\theta}=\cos11\theta+i\sin11\theta$.

Option A comes from adding $5\theta+2\theta$ and ignoring the exponent $-3$; option B comes from reading the exponent as $+3$ ($e^{5i\theta}/e^{6i\theta}=e^{-i\theta}$).

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Suppose $f(0.6)=0.7$ and $f'(0.6)=10.6$. If $x_1=0.6$ is the first approximation to the root of $f(x)=0$ then using the Newton-Raphson method, a second approximate root $x_2$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Newton-Raphson iteration is $x_{n+1}=x_n-\dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}$ (tangent at $x_n$ meets the $x$-axis). With $x_1=0.6$: $x_2=0.6-\dfrac{f(0.6)}{f'(0.6)}=0.6-\dfrac{0.7}{10.6}\approx0.534$.

Options A and B have the wrong sign; B and D invert the quotient (they use $f'/f$).

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given the matrix $\mathbf A$, where $\mathbf A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1\\0&3&1\\0&-1&4\end{pmatrix}$, the determinant of $\mathbf A^{\mathrm T}$, where $\mathbf A^{\mathrm T}$ is the transpose of $\mathbf A$, is
questions.corrige_markdown:
A matrix and its transpose have the same determinant: $\det\mathbf A^{\mathrm T}=\det\mathbf A$.

Expand $\det\mathbf A$ along the first column (only the entry $1$ is non-zero): $\det\mathbf A=1\cdot\begin{vmatrix}3&1\\-1&4\end{vmatrix}=3\cdot4-1\cdot(-1)=12+1=13$.

Option A ($12$) forgets that $-1\times1$ contributes $+1$ (sign error).

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The image of the line $y=3x$ under the transformation matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$ is the line
questions.corrige_markdown:
A general point of the line is $(t,3t)$. Its image is
$\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}t\\3t\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2t+3t\\t+9t\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}5t\\10t\end{pmatrix}$.

So the image points $(x',y')=(5t,10t)$ satisfy $y'=2x'$: the image line is $y=2x$ (a line through the origin is mapped to a line through the origin, since the determinant $2\cdot3-1\cdot1=5\neq0$).

Option C ($y=\frac{5}{10}x$) swaps the roles of the two image coordinates; A and B are not the ratio $10t/5t$.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
![fig-1](gce-al-pm-mechanics-2026-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

The shaded region, in Fig. 1, represents
questions.corrige_markdown:
In Fig. 1 the circles $A$ and $B$ overlap. The shaded region is the part of $A$ that lies outside $B$: the lens where the two circles overlap is not shaded and the part of $B$ outside $A$ is not shaded. That region is "in $A$ and not in $B$", i.e. $A\cap B'$.

Options A and D are empty sets: $A'\cap(A\cap B)$ asks for elements both outside $A$ and inside $A$, and $B'\cap(A\cap B)$ asks for elements both outside $B$ and inside $B$. Option B, $A'\cap B$, is the part of $B$ outside $A$, which is the unshaded crescent on the right.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION B: MECHANICS**

The position vector of a particle is $\mathbf r=\left[(3\sin3t)\mathbf i+(2\cos2t)\mathbf j\right]$ m at time $t$ s. The initial velocity of the particle is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The velocity is the derivative of the position vector: $\mathbf v=\dfrac{d\mathbf r}{dt}=(9\cos3t)\mathbf i-(4\sin2t)\mathbf j\ \ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

At $t=0$: $\cos0=1$ and $\sin0=0$, so $\mathbf v(0)=9\mathbf i-0\,\mathbf j=9\mathbf i\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

Options B and C have a $\mathbf j$-component of $\pm4$, which would need $\cos2t$ in the derivative instead of $\sin2t$. Option D gives only the magnitude $9\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (a speed): the question asks for a velocity, which is a vector with direction $\mathbf i$.

**Answer: A.**

themes: elastic strings and potential energy mechanics
questions.enonce_markdown: When an elastic string is stretched to a length of $1.8$ m, the tension in the string is $14$ N. Given that the modulus of elasticity of the string is $28$ N, the natural length of the string is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Hooke's law: $T=\dfrac{\lambda x}{l}$ where $\lambda=28$ N is the modulus of elasticity, $l$ the natural length and $x=1.8-l$ the extension.

$14=\dfrac{28(1.8-l)}{l}\Rightarrow14l=28(1.8-l)\Rightarrow l=2(1.8-l)\Rightarrow3l=3.6\Rightarrow l=1.2$ m.

Check: extension $=1.8-1.2=0.6$ m, tension $=28\cdot\dfrac{0.6}{1.2}=14$ N. Option A ($1.6$ m) would give a tension $28\cdot\frac{0.2}{1.6}=3.5$ N.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The speeds of a car during $8$ seconds of braking are given in the table below.

| Time, $t$ s | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Speed, $v$ $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ | 30 | 27 | 22 | 14 | 0 |

Using the trapezium rule, the distance moved by the car in coming to rest is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The distance is the area under the speed-time graph: $s=\displaystyle\int_0^8v\,dt$. There are $5$ ordinates, so $4$ strips of width $h=2$:
$s\approx\dfrac h2\Big[v_0+v_4+2(v_1+v_2+v_3)\Big]=\dfrac22\Big[30+0+2(27+22+14)\Big]=30+126=156$ m.

Check strip by strip: $\frac{30+27}{2}\cdot2+\frac{27+22}{2}\cdot2+\frac{22+14}{2}\cdot2+\frac{14+0}{2}\cdot2=57+49+36+14=156$.

The wrong options come from slips in the rule: C ($93$ m) is the plain sum of the five speeds; B ($78$ m) is half of the correct value (the factor $\frac12$ used instead of $\frac h2=1$); D ($186$ m) doubles the first speed as well ($2\times93$).

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Fig. 2 shows the forces acting on a uniform ladder $AB$, of length $12$ m, resting in limiting equilibrium. A man $M$ ascends the ladder.

![fig-2](gce-al-pm-mechanics-2026-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)

The ladder will begin to slip when $M$ has ascended up the ladder a distance

*Options as printed:* A) $9$ m   B) $6$ m   C) $3$ m   D) $4$ m
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Reading of Fig. 2 (printed data).** The ladder $AB$ (length $12$ m) leans against the vertical wall at $B$ and rests on the ground at $A$; the angle between the ladder and the wall at $B$ is $45^\circ$, so the ladder makes $45^\circ$ with the ground. Forces: at $B$, the wall reaction $S=5$ N horizontal, pointing away from the wall; at $A$, the normal reaction $R=15$ N upwards and the friction $F=5$ N horizontal, towards the wall; the weight of the man $10$ N at $M$; the weight of the uniform ladder $5$ N at its midpoint, which is $6$ m from $A$.

**Consistency check.** Horizontal: $S=F=5$ N. Vertical: $R=10+5=15$ N. Limiting friction $F=\mu R$ gives $\mu=\tfrac13$.

**Moments about $A$.** Let $d$ be the distance $AM$ along the ladder (the distance ascended from the foot). With the ladder at $45^\circ$, the horizontal distance of a point at distance $s$ from $A$ is $s\sin45^\circ$ and the height of $B$ above the ground is $12\cos45^\circ$. Taking moments about $A$ (the wall reaction tends to turn the ladder one way, the weights the other way):
$$
S\cdot12\cos45^\circ=5\cdot6\sin45^\circ+10\cdot d\sin45^\circ
$$
Since $\sin45^\circ=\cos45^\circ$: $5\cdot12=30+10d$, so $10d=30$ and $d=3$ m.

**Check about $B$.** The man is then $12-3=9$ m from $B$: $R\cdot12\sin45^\circ-F\cdot12\cos45^\circ=5\cdot6\sin45^\circ+10\cdot9\sin45^\circ$ gives $180-60=30+90$, i.e. $120=120$.

So the ladder is on the point of slipping when $M$ has climbed $3$ m from the foot $A$. Option A ($9$ m) is the distance of $M$ from the top $B$ at that moment (or a measurement from the wrong end); B ($6$ m) is the midpoint, where only the ladder's own weight acts.

**Intended answer: C ($3$ m).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: A girl on a ship, whose velocity is $(4\mathbf i-7\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ is watching a boat whose velocity is $(-8\mathbf i-2\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The speed of the boat as it appears to the girl on the ship is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The velocity of the boat relative to the ship is $\mathbf v_{B/S}=\mathbf v_B-\mathbf v_S=(-8\mathbf i-2\mathbf j)-(4\mathbf i-7\mathbf j)=(-12\mathbf i+5\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

The speed it appears to have is the magnitude of this relative velocity: $|\mathbf v_{B/S}|=\sqrt{(-12)^2+5^2}=\sqrt{169}=13\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

Option A is the relative velocity itself, a vector: it is not a speed, so it does not answer the question as worded. Option B is the velocity of the ship relative to the boat (opposite vector). Option D is $|\mathbf v_B|-|\mathbf v_S|$, the difference of the speeds, which is not the relative speed.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The speed $v$ of a particle moving in a straight line from rest $t$ s after passing through a fixed point $O$ is $v=(6t^2-5t+3)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The distance of the particle from $O$ when $t=4$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The particle passes through $O$ at $t=0$, so the distance from $O$ at time $t$ is $s=\displaystyle\int_0^tv\,dt$ as long as the particle does not turn back. Here $v=6t^2-5t+3$ has discriminant $25-72<0$, so $v>0$ for all $t$: the particle always moves forward and the distance from $O$ equals the distance travelled.

$s=\displaystyle\int_0^4(6t^2-5t+3)\,dt=\left[2t^3-\tfrac52t^2+3t\right]_0^4=128-40+12=100$ m.

Check: $v(4)=96-20+3=79\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ is the speed at $t=4$, not the distance. Note: the formula gives $v(0)=3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so the particle is not literally at rest at $O$ at $t=0$; the wording "from rest" is read as "starting its motion at $t=0$" and does not change the integral.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The work done by a force $\mathbf F$, where $\mathbf F=(\mathbf i+2\mathbf j+3\mathbf k)$ N, which moves its point of application from a point $P$ with position vector $\mathbf r_P=(3\mathbf i+4\mathbf j+5\mathbf k)$ m to another point $Q$ whose position vector is $\mathbf r_Q=(7\mathbf i+6\mathbf j+5\mathbf k)$ m is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Work done by a constant force: $W=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf d$ where $\mathbf d=\mathbf r_Q-\mathbf r_P=(7-3)\mathbf i+(6-4)\mathbf j+(5-5)\mathbf k=(4\mathbf i+2\mathbf j)$ m.

$W=(1,2,3)\cdot(4,2,0)=4+4+0=8$ J.

Option C ($-8$ J) comes from taking the displacement the wrong way round ($\mathbf r_P-\mathbf r_Q$).

**Answer: D.**

themes: motion of a vehicle with resistance
questions.enonce_markdown: A car of mass $1{,}200$ kg moving with speed $12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ has its engine working at $54$ kW up a road inclined at an angle $\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac15\right)$ to the horizontal. The non-gravitational resistance to the motion of the car is $300$ N. Taking $g$ as $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, the acceleration of the car is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Take the direction of motion (up the slope) as positive.

Driving force: $F=\dfrac Pv=\dfrac{54\,000}{12}=4500$ N.

Forces along the slope: driving force $F$ up the slope; resistance $300$ N down the slope; component of the weight down the slope $mg\sin\alpha=1200\cdot10\cdot\dfrac15=2400$ N.

Newton's second law: $4500-300-2400=1200\,a$, so $1800=1200\,a$ and $a=1.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ (up the slope).

The main trap is forgetting the weight component $mg\sin\alpha$, which gives $\dfrac{4500-300}{1200}=3.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ (option C). Forgetting the resistance instead would give $\dfrac{4500-2400}{1200}=1.75$, which is not an option; A and D do not come from a consistent balance of forces.

**Answer: B.**

themes: centre of mass of composite bodies
questions.enonce_markdown: Three particles of weight $7$ N, $9$ N and $4$ N have position vector $(4\mathbf i+\mathbf j)$ m, $3\mathbf j$ m and $(3\mathbf i+4\mathbf j)$ m respectively. The position vector of their centre of mass is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The weights are proportional to the masses ($g$ is the same for all three), so the centre of mass is the weighted mean $\bar{\mathbf r}=\dfrac{\sum w_i\mathbf r_i}{\sum w_i}$ with $\sum w_i=7+9+4=20$ N.

$\sum w_i\mathbf r_i=7(4\mathbf i+\mathbf j)+9(3\mathbf j)+4(3\mathbf i+4\mathbf j)=(28\mathbf i+7\mathbf j)+27\mathbf j+(12\mathbf i+16\mathbf j)=40\mathbf i+50\mathbf j$.

$\bar{\mathbf r}=\dfrac{40\mathbf i+50\mathbf j}{20}=\left(2\mathbf i+\dfrac52\mathbf j\right)$ m.

Option A is the unweighted average of the three positions; C is the total moment $\sum w_i\mathbf r_i$ (not divided by $20$); D divides the unweighted sum $7\mathbf i+8\mathbf j$ by $20$.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Fig. 3 shows two particles $P$ and $Q$ hanging freely and connected by a light inextensible string passing over a fixed smooth pulley.

![fig-3](gce-al-pm-mechanics-2026-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)

The system is released from rest. Taking $g$ as $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, the acceleration of $P$ and the tension in the string are
questions.corrige_markdown:
From the figure: the weight of $P$ is $10$ N and the weight of $Q$ is $40$ N. With $g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ the masses are $m_P=1$ kg and $m_Q=4$ kg. (The stem prints the unit of $g$ as $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; it is read as $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.)

The string is light and inextensible and the pulley is smooth, so the tension $T$ is the same on both sides and both particles have accelerations of the same magnitude $a$. $Q$ is heavier, so $Q$ moves down and $P$ moves up.

Equation for $P$ (upwards positive): $T-10=1\cdot a$.
Equation for $Q$ (downwards positive): $40-T=4a$.

Adding: $30=5a$, so $a=6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Then $T=10+6=16$ N. Check with $Q$: $40-16=24=4\times6$.

Options B and C have $a=10$ (free fall), which would need $T=0$; A has the right acceleration but $T=8$ N, which is not consistent with $T-10=a$.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle of mass $4$ kg which is moving in horizontal straight line with velocity $15\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ strikes a vertical wall. If the coefficient of restitution between the particle and the wall is $\dfrac23$ then the magnitude of the impulse experienced by the particle is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Take the direction towards the wall as positive. Before impact the velocity is $+15\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Newton's law of restitution for a fixed wall: the speed after impact is $e\times$ the speed before, so the particle rebounds at $\dfrac23\cdot15=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ away from the wall, velocity $-10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

Impulse = change in momentum: $I=m(v-u)=4\left(-10-15\right)=-100$ N s. Its magnitude is $100$ N s (directed away from the wall); equivalently $I=m(1+e)u=4\cdot\dfrac53\cdot15=100$ N s.

Option C ($60$ N s) is the momentum before impact only; B ($40$ N s) is the rebound momentum only; neither is the change.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle is projected from a point $O$ with initial speed $(15\sqrt3\,\mathbf i+15\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Taking [$g$] as $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ its position vector after $2$ seconds is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The printed "initial speed" is a vector, i.e. the initial velocity $\mathbf u=(15\sqrt3\,\mathbf i+15\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ with $\mathbf i$ horizontal and $\mathbf j$ vertically upwards (the letter $g$ is missing in the printed sentence; it is read as $g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ downwards, the only value given).

Horizontal motion (no acceleration): $x=15\sqrt3\cdot2=30\sqrt3$ m.
Vertical motion (acceleration $-10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$): $y=15\cdot2-\tfrac12\cdot10\cdot2^2=30-20=10$ m.

So $\mathbf r=(30\sqrt3\,\mathbf i+10\mathbf j)$ m. Check with the vector formula $\mathbf r=\mathbf ut+\tfrac12\mathbf gt^2$ with $\mathbf g=-10\mathbf j$: $2(15\sqrt3\,\mathbf i+15\mathbf j)+\tfrac12(-10\mathbf j)(4)=30\sqrt3\,\mathbf i+30\mathbf j-20\mathbf j$.

Options A, C and D put the numbers $15\sqrt3$, $30\sqrt3$, $10$ and $5$ in the wrong components or use the wrong time (the $\pm5$ is $\tfrac12gt^2$ taken at $t=1$ instead of $t=2$).

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
One end of an inelastic string is fixed to a point $O$ and the other end is attached to a particle of mass $4$ kg. The particle is kept in a horizontal circle of radius $8$ m. Given that the center of the circle is $2.5$ m vertically below $O$ and the tension in the string is $128$ N, the angular speed of the particle is

*Options as printed:* A) $16\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$   B) $16\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$   C) $2\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$   D) $2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Set-up.** The string joins $O$ to the particle, which moves in a horizontal circle of radius $r=8$ m whose centre is $2.5$ m below $O$. The string length is $L=\sqrt{8^2+2.5^2}=\sqrt{70.25}\approx8.38$ m, and it makes an angle $\theta$ with the vertical where $\sin\theta=\dfrac{8}{L}$ and $\cos\theta=\dfrac{2.5}{L}$.

**Horizontal equation** (the horizontal component of the tension provides the centripetal force): $T\sin\theta=m r\omega^2$, so $\omega^2=\dfrac{T\sin\theta}{mr}=\dfrac{T}{mL}=\dfrac{128}{4\times8.38}\approx3.82$ and $\omega\approx1.95\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

**Vertical equation** (no vertical acceleration): $T\cos\theta=mg$ would need $T\cos\theta=128\times\dfrac{2.5}{8.38}\approx38.2$ N against $mg\approx39.2$ to $40$ N: the printed data are therefore not exactly consistent with each other (over-determined), and the result above depends on which equation is used.

**Intended answer.** The data are built so that $T=mr\omega^2$ gives exactly $\omega=\sqrt{\dfrac{128}{4\cdot8}}=2\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ (as if the tension were the full centripetal force, i.e. ignoring the $2.5$ m depth). The exact value with the given geometry, $1.95\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$, is not among the options, but option C ($2\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$) is the only option with the unit of an angular speed and the right order of magnitude (A and D are in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, which is a linear speed; B is $8$ times too large).

**Intended answer: C ($2\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

themes: simple harmonic motion of a particle
questions.enonce_markdown: A particle of mass $m$ moving along a straight line $Ox$ is subjected to a force $16mx$ acting towards the origin $O$. Given that the particle starts from rest when $x=5$ m, the speed of the particle as it passes through the $O$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The force acts towards $O$, so with $x$ measured from $O$: $m\ddot x=-16mx$, i.e. $\ddot x=-16x$. Write $\ddot x=v\dfrac{dv}{dx}$:
$v\dfrac{dv}{dx}=-16x\Rightarrow\dfrac{v^2}{2}=-8x^2+c$.

At $x=5$, $v=0$: $c=200$, so $v^2=400-16x^2$. At $O$ ($x=0$): $v^2=400$, so $v=20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

Check (simple harmonic motion): $\omega^2=16$, $\omega=4$ rad/s, amplitude $a=5$ m, maximum speed (at the centre) $\omega a=20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Check with work-energy: work done by the force from $x=5$ to $0$ is $\displaystyle\int_0^5 16mx\,dx=200m=\tfrac12mv^2$, so $v^2=400$.

Option D ($10\sqrt2$) is $\sqrt{200}$, obtained by forgetting the factor $\tfrac12$ in $\tfrac12mv^2$.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If it is known that the events $A$ and $B$ are collectively exhaustive and independent, the true statement is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Collectively exhaustive means that at least one of the events occurs: $P(A\cup B)=1$.

Addition rule: $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$. Independence: $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\times P(B)$.

Therefore $1=P(A)+P(B)-P(A)P(B)$, i.e. $P(A)+P(B)=1+P(A)\times P(B)$.

Option D, $P(A)+P(B)=1$, would hold for mutually exclusive and exhaustive events (complementary events), which cannot be independent unless one has probability $0$ or $1$. Option B has the wrong sign of the product term; option A would give $P(A)(1-P(B))=-P(B)$, whose left side is $\geq0$ and right side $\leq0$, forcing $P(A)=P(B)=0$, which contradicts "exhaustive".

**Answer: C.**
